title: Advanced TypeScript with Matt (LIVE)
summary: Matt Pocock live-streams an hour of advanced TypeScript, starting with warm-up exercises from the type-challenges repo and escalating to a full reading of a type-level bubble sort. He solves Concat with variadic tuple spread in minutes, wrestles the Includes challenge (where the naive T[number] union check fails on edge cases like boolean and object literals) and ultimately adopts a community solution using recursive conditional types plus a custom Equal type with covariant-contravariant tricks. Between exercises he demos his TypeScript Error Translator, which converts raw compiler errors into plain English. The finale is a line-by-line walkthrough of Anurag Hazra's bubble sort written entirely in the type system, explaining the n-tuple trick for doing arithmetic with tuple lengths, a namespace used as a type-class, infer-based tuple destructuring, and underscore-prefixed accumulator generics that act as local variables.
what_you_learn: You learn how to actually read type-level code - the mental models that make crazy generics legible: extends as an assignability check, numbers encoded as tuple lengths, recursion via self-referencing conditional types, and extra defaulted generics as saved local variables. These are the exact techniques used by libraries like Zod, tRPC, and ts-tool-belt, so being able to follow them demystifies the type errors and autocomplete you rely on daily - and the type-challenges repo plus the error translator are two immediately usable practice tools.

skills.name: TypeScript Type System
skills.description: Writing algorithms (sort, arithmetic, search) in TypeScript's type system using conditional types, recursion, and tuple manipulation.

learnings.title: Concat solved in minutes with variadic tuple spread
learnings.detail: The type-challenges Concat exercise asks you to reimplement JS array.concat in the type system. The solution is two constrained generics - TFirst extends any[], TSecond extends any[] - and a single spread: [...TFirst, ...TSecond]. The extends constraints are essential: without them TypeScript complains the type 'must be an array type', and constraining at the generic level is terser than a conditional-type fallback (TFirst extends any[] ? ... : never). Matt notes he 'stumbled on' the solution - variadic tuple types do a lot of heavy lifting for very little syntax - and verified it matched the top community solutions.

learnings.title: extends means assignable-to, and direction matters
learnings.detail: Working through Includes, Matt drills the core intuition: A extends B answers 'can I pass A where B is expected?' - string extends any is true, but string extends '123' is false because you can't assign a general string to a literal slot. He frames it as the assignability of function arguments: myFunk('123') works when the parameter is string, but not the reverse. This resolves which side of the conditional the union goes on: to check whether an item could be a member of the array union, you check TItem extends TArray[number] - the narrower candidate extends the wider union.

learnings.title: The naive Includes check fails, and the real solution is a recursive reduce with a custom Equal
learnings.detail: Matt's first Includes attempt - TArray[number] extends TItem - passed simple cases but broke on edge cases: an array containing boolean breaks it, and structural comparisons mistake distinct object literals for matches because extends is assignability, not equality. His verdict: 'no one seems to have got this right' with the naive approach. The accepted community solution walks the tuple recursively like a JS reduce: T extends [infer First, ...infer Rest] ? (First and TItem both extend each other ? true : Includes<Rest, TItem>) : false. Exact object equality requires a custom Equal type built on covariant-contravariant function-parameter tricks - the kind of machinery you import from a library like ts-tool-belt rather than write yourself.

learnings.title: The TypeScript Error Translator turns compiler errors into plain English
learnings.detail: Matt demos a tool he has been building: paste any TypeScript error and it outputs a plain-English translation with a shareable link. Example: 'Conversion of type number to type string may be a mistake because neither type sufficiently overlaps with the other' becomes 'You can't use as to convert a number into a string - they don't share enough in common', plus the common cause (produced by 'hello' as number). For junior-mid devs, tooling that translates error messages is high-leverage: the compiler already knows what is wrong, and the barrier is only the jargon.

learnings.title: N-tuples: do arithmetic by encoding numbers as tuple lengths
learnings.detail: The foundation of the type-level bubble sort is a namespace M acting like a type-class (only exported members are the public API). TypeScript has no numeric comparisons, so the trick is: NTuple<N> builds a tuple of length N, turning a number into a countable structure; Length<T> reads a tuple's length back into a number. Addition becomes spreading two n-tuples into a new tuple and taking its length; subtraction infers the tail of the longer tuple and measures what remains (going below zero yields never, since you can't subtract more members than exist). Once you grasp this plumbing, the rest of the algorithm is ordinary array manipulation.

learnings.title: Comparing numbers: equality check, then subtraction sign
learnings.detail: The comparator in M works in two steps. First, n1 extends n2 ? false - if the two are assignable (equal), return false. Otherwise compute n2-as-n1 (subtract and infer the remainder): if the result is never - meaning the subtraction underflowed, so n2 is the larger number - return true; otherwise return false. Matt walks concrete numbers (2 vs 4, 1 vs 0) to show the logic checks out, noting the comparison is wrapped in a tuple 'so it doesn't expand' in tooltips. This is the classic a-greater-than-b-via-underflow pattern from type-level programming folklore.

learnings.title: Underscore generics are local variables, and recursion walks the array
learnings.detail: In the bubble sort itself, the public API takes a single generic, but the type declares _Current with a default - an accumulator slot that stores intermediate state (here: how many elements remain to process), a standard trick for 'saving a local variable' in the type system. The body pattern-matches with infer: T extends [...infer FirstElm, infer SecondElm, ...infer Rest], then if the comparator says the second is larger, emits [Second, First, ...bubble-sort the rest], otherwise [First, Second, ...rest] - a self-referencing recursive call, exactly like a JS function calling itself with a smaller input. The base case fires when the element count reaches one.

learnings.title: How to practice: type-challenges repo, community solutions, and a graded path
learnings.detail: Matt's own practice workflow is visible throughout: take a challenge from the type-challenges repo (install @type-challenges/utils for the Equal and Expect test helpers), solve it in your editor against the failing test cases, then check out other people's solutions to compare - he found his Concat matched the top community answer. He caveats that the repo's difficulty ordering is imperfect ('some are pretty easy and some are really really hard' - Includes humbled him live), and mentions wanting to author more graded, easier challenges as part of his course. Takeaway: reading solutions you couldn't write is a legitimate and productive mode of practice at this level.

key_points: A extends B reads as 'A is assignable to B' - the direction is everything.
Variadic tuples: [...TFirst, ...TSecond] reimplements array.concat at the type level.
extends checks assignability, not equality - comparing object literals needs a custom Equal type.
No numbers in the type system? Encode them as tuple lengths: NTuple builds, Length reads back.
Subtraction is inferring the tail of a tuple; underflow (never) doubles as a less-than test.
Extra defaulted generics like _Current are how you save local variables inside a type.
T extends [infer First, ...infer Rest] is type-level array destructuring, enabling recursion.
Reading solutions you couldn't write is legitimate practice - even Matt bailed on Includes.
The TypeScript Error Translator exists: paste a compiler error, get plain English back.
